chunks: Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār said:

I said to Abū Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him): A man said, 'He is a Jew or a Christian, if he does not do such and such,' so he (the Imam) said, 'What a bad thing he said, and there is no obligation upon him.'

key_terms.بِئْسَ مَا قَالَ: What a bad thing he said
key_terms.لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ: There is no obligation/penalty upon him

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a conditional oath or statement if the condition is not met, according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a conditional statement made by a Jew or Christian is linguistically valid but religiously non-binding, meaning no expiation (*kaffarah*) is required if the condition is not met. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential distinction between the semantic validity of an oath and its legal enforceability, particularly when the speaker is not bound by Islamic ritual law. It underscores the principle that *al-yamin* (oath) in this context does not incur penalty unless explicitly intended as a binding religious vow.
